findings.title: Denial cache key collides with the permission cache key
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey produces namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>, which shares the namespace.perm_ prefix with userPermCacheKey (namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>). Both caches wrap the same underlying cache.Cache. Because the denial key is longer, an exact collision is unlikely in practice, but the shared prefix is fragile. The unescaped '_' separators also let different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key, for example name 'a_b' with parent 'c' versus name 'a' with parent 'b_c'. Use a distinct prefix such as '.perm_denial_' and an unambiguous separator.

findings.title: Denial cache blocks access for 30s after a permission is granted
findings.body: A denial is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s). If the same user is denied on a resource and then gets access (for example, creating a dashboard or folder), every Check for that (action, name, parent) returns denied from the denial cache until it expires. The cache is checked before the DB requery, so this can reintroduce the stale-permission problem the PR is meant to fix. It matters most for a Check issued just before creation, for example an existence probe. The denial entry is never invalidated.

findings.title: Cache lookup errors abort or skew the fallback path and metrics
findings.body: getCachedIdentityPermissions calls GetUserIdentifiers, which can hit the DB. Any error from it is silently swallowed and the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which repeats the same lookup. The permission-cache metric is also double counted: it is incremented 'true' on denial-cache hits and 'false' on every non-allowed cached result. A cache hit that results in a deny, followed by a DB requery, is counted as a miss, which makes the metric misleading.

findings.title: Cache-hit test case removed and cacheHit field left unused
findings.body: The cache-hit case was removed from TestService_getUserPermissions, but the cacheHit field and its branches remain as dead code. The new tests do not assert that the DB is not called on a cache hit, or that a denial is stored after a DB deny. There is no test that a denial is written to permDenialCache.
